series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/4] mm/damon: defensively skip zone device folios in damon_get_folio()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds an explicit check to the damon_get_folio() function to reject zone device folios, making it consistent with other mm walkers that follow this convention. The existing implicit exclusion of ZONE_DEVICE memory through pfn_to_online_page() and folio_test_lru() is maintained, but now there's a uniform guarantee across all callers. This change improves code consistency and makes the behavior more predictable.

review_comments.author: SJ Park
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch's addition of folio_is_zone_device() to damon_get_folio() is not sufficient, as it does not handle the case where a zone device folio has already been obtained and its reference count is non-zero.

Reviewer SJ Park expressed concern that adding an explicit check for zone device folios in damon_get_folio() may be unnecessary and confusing, suggesting instead to use CONFIG_DAMON_DEBUG_SANITY with a clear explanation.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Gregory,


On Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:47:11 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

---

Thank you for checking this and sharing this nice patch!

However, I'm not very sure adding a call that not really required for only
making it looks consistent with others is the right choice.  I'm especially
concerned if this will confuse future readers including myself.

If this is a hardening purpose, we have CONFIG_DAMON_DEBUG_SANITY for the
purpose.  What about using it with a good comment explaining why we doing that?


Thanks,
SJ

[...]

review_comments.author: Gregory Price (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that zone device checks are missing in some areas and decided to add explicit checks everywhere, including in damon_get_folio(), to make it clear there's a zone device interaction, even if presently unreachable.
review_comments.raw_body:
It's actually two fold:

  1) make zone_device more consistently handled across mm/
  2) make these checks possible to abstract out later

In the private node work - every location that we'd need to filter
folios based on private node membership is a zone_device check.

Where zone device checks are missing (like here) there's some other
implicit reason (specific to zone device) that allows it to be avoided.

I pointed out in the sashiko feedback that DAMON depends on a check
for folio->pgmap in the hotplug code.  This is all quite fragile, and
we can see that at least one patch in this series fixes an actual bug.

It seemed warranted to go audit every service and add the zone_device
checks to make it clear there's a zone device interaction - even if
presently unreachable - should some silent, implicit filter change.

The goal is to come back around and replace these with something like:

    bool folio_allows_mm_op(struct folio *folio,
                            enum node_states feature)
    {
        if (folio_is_zone_device(folio) ||
            !node_state(folio_nid(folio), feature));
    }

    - if (folio_is_zone_device(folio))
    + if (folio_allows_mm_op(folio, N_MEMORY_DAMON))

If we ever get to folios having memdesc flags beyond page flags,
this also gives us a single mm-wide location for these kinds of
checks in the future.

~Gregory

review_comments.author: SJ Park
review_comments.summary: Reviewer suggested adding a check under CONFIG_DAMON_DEBUG_SANITY first, with good comments, before replacing it with folio_allows_mm_ops()
review_comments.raw_body:
Thank you for kindly explaining the motivation.

So, what do you think about adding the check under CONFIG_DAMON_DEBUG_SANITY
with good comments at the moment, and later converting to folio_allows_mm_ops()
together?


Thanks,
SJ

[...]

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/4] mm/huge_memory: skip zone device folios in madvise_free_huge_pmd()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses issues in the huge_memory module by skipping zone device folios in madvise_free_huge_pmd(). The current implementation resolves the folio backing a PMD via pmd_folio() and marks it lazyfree without checking for zone device memory. This can lead to incorrect behavior, especially when dealing with device-private THPs. The patch introduces a check to bail out when the folio is a zone device folio, ensuring that these special cases are handled correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/4] mm/madvise: skip zone device folios in cold/pageout PMD range
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses issues in the madvise_cold_or_pageout_pte_range function, which resolves folio backing a PMD and ages or reclaims it without checking for zone device memory. The current implementation does not cover all cases of zone device memory, leading to potential double-put bugs. This patch specifically skips ZONE_DEVICE folios during MADV_COLD/PAGEOUT operations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/4] mm/mempolicy: skip zone device folios when queueing folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses an issue where zone device folios are not properly filtered when queueing folios in the mm/mempolicy code. The patches modify three walkers (queue_folios_pte_range, queue_folios_pmd, and queue_folios_hugetlb) to skip zone device folios by adding explicit checks for folio_is_zone_device(). This ensures that zone device memory is not mistakenly added to the migration pagelist.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series adds checks to prevent zone device memory from being accessed or modified by various Linux kernel functions, including madvise and mempolicy walkers. The changes are aimed at preventing potential issues that could arise when dealing with ZONE_DEVICE memory. The patches fall into two categories: genuine gaps in existing checks and defensive/consistency additions. No locking or refcount changes are involved, as the checks are placed after the folio is resolved and before it is acted upon. This series is a correctness/hardening cleanup found by inspection.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/5] btrfs: use an on-stack path in btrfs_insert_orphan_item()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the performance and reliability of Btrfs by reducing memory allocation failures in critical paths, such as btrfs_insert_orphan_item(). The first patch in the series addresses a specific issue where a path allocation failure can lead to a transaction abort. It does this by allocating a btrfs_path on the stack instead of dynamically.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/5] btrfs: split btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() into prealloc and commit phases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() function into three separate functions: prealloc, commit, and free. The prealloc function allocates memory for a delayed node and item before modifying the B-tree, allowing -ENOMEM to be returned cleanly if allocation fails. The commit function populates the item data and inserts it into the rb-tree, while the free function releases pre-allocated resources in case of failure. This refactoring improves error handling and reduces the risk of aborting transactions due to memory allocation failures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/5] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index before btree modification
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the Btrfs file system by pre-allocating delayed directory indices before modifying the btree. This change prevents ENOMEM failures from leaving the btree in an inconsistent state, which could only be resolved by aborting the transaction. The patch introduces a new parameter to the btrfs_insert_dir_item function for caller-provided pre-allocation and removes a wrapper function that was no longer needed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/5] btrfs: handle ENOMEM from btrfs_insert_dir_item() without aborting
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs kernel code to handle ENOMEM errors from btrfs_insert_dir_item() without aborting the transaction. Instead of aborting, it clears the nlink count and orphans the newly-created inode when memory is exhausted during file system operations such as create(), mkdir(), mknod(), symlink(), and link(). This change allows for more graceful handling of memory pressure situations, preventing potential filesystem corruption.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 5/5] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index for non-overwrite rename
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the Btrfs file system by pre-allocating a delayed directory index before performing non-overwrite renames, allowing for early detection of ENOMEM errors and preventing potential data corruption. The patch introduces a new function to pre-allocate the delayed dir index and modifies existing functions to handle this new parameter. It also preserves the current behavior for overwrite renames by continuing with the transaction even if an ENOMEM error is encountered.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a long-standing issue in the Btrfs file system where memory allocation failures can cause the file system to abort. The patches rework the code to perform memory allocations before critical points, preventing aborts due to ENOMEM errors. This includes changes to directory morphing and orphan handling, with additional tests added to exercise the new behavior. While not all potential cases are covered, this series is designed to work in conjunction with other patches to address remaining issues.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses the issue of stale memory cgroup (memcg) stats causing premature OOM kills by proposing a solution to reduce the overhead of updating and flushing these statistics. The idea is for memcg to accumulate updates on a per-CPU basis, then propagate them up to a global atomic counter when it reaches a certain threshold, eliminating the need for frequent flushing. This approach aims to scale better for large machines with many cores and focuses on reducing the number of stats that require flushing, specifically NR_FILE_DIRTY and NR_WRITEBACK in the writeback case.

review_comments.summary: Author acknowledges that the flush operation would need to touch multiple cachelines per CPU on a large machine, but does not provide a clear resolution or plan for addressing this issue.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed noted that the patch may not address premature OOM kills due to stale stats in the vmscan path, citing a test where VMs experienced OOM kills after the ratelimited flush, and suggested further investigation is needed.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed questioned the trade-off between update and read performance in memcg stats, suggesting that increasing the cost of updates could improve the manageability of the read path, which is becoming slow in some cases.

The reviewer pointed out that memcg stats perform similar per-CPU counting and thresholding as vmstat, but with a cgroup hierarchy, which requires reading hierarchical stats including children. They suggested replacing the current flushing logic with updating the stat on each parent or forgoing the rstat flushing logic altogether.

Reviewer suggested side-stepping the flushing issue by either keeping track of CPUs with updates via rstat or propagating per-CPU stat updates when reaching a threshold, similar to how vmstat handles batching
review_comments.raw_body:
I don't think we had time to look into this closely. We have a test
that runs VMs with some memory pressure / reclaim, and we observed OOM
kills in that test after the ratelimited flush in the vmscan path.
Whether or not this translates to additional OOM kills in our prod is
currently unknown, but it's a signal that reclaim effectiveness may be
negatively affected in some cases.

---

Yeah I think we generally want to keep updates faster than reads,
because some of them are also in latency-sensitive paths like
networking. However, since reads are becoming too slow in some cases,
the question here is whether we can afford some extra cost on the
update side (to iterate parent per-CPU counters) to make the read path
more manageable.

---

The memcg stats perform similar per-CPU counting and thresholding. The
main difference from vmstat AFAICT is the cgroup hierarchy. In vmstat
we have per-CPU counters and a global atomic counter for each stat.
For memcg, we have the same for each cgroup, then we also have a
cgroup tree. When we read the stats of a cgroup, we usually want the
hierarchical stats including all of its children, so we can't just
read the global counter.

We use rstat, a cgroup framework that keeps track of which cgroups
have updates on which CPUs, and then memcg has thresholding logic on
top to only flush if the number of pending updates exceeds a
threshold. Essentially, if the magnitude updates on a CPU exceeds
MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH, we add it to a global per-memcg counter. We only
flush if that global per-memcg counter has > NR_CPUS *
MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH updates. So in theory I think we tolerate up to 2 *
NR_CPUS * MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH of stale stats (combined for all the
stats).

See memcg_rstat_updated() and memcg_vmstats_needs_flush() for this logic.

Looking at this code again, it made me realize that we already iterate
the per-CPU stats_updates on every update to increment the number of
pending stats on this CPU. I wonder if we can replace this with
actually updating the stat on each parent, then the flush path only
needs to accumulate CPU counters. Or maybe as you mention, we update
the global per-memcg counter when updates on a CPU exceed a threshold,
and forgo the rstat flushing logic completely.

---

Probably not (hence I called it radical), but I think this can be
side-stepped by either keeping the tracking of CPUs that have updates
via rstat (or similar), or just propagating the per-CPU stat updates
when they reach a threshold like vmstat.

Yeah it has become complicated. The other concern Sashiko raised is the case
where the destination node's objcg has reached/reparented to root and the source
node's objcg is still not root. Since we skip root page counters for LRU pages,
this can unbalance them. It's one more check to add.

 		return proc_dointvec_minmax(table, write, buffer, length, ppos);
